articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Send a Work Email at Night or on the Weekend?
articles.content:
我的一位编辑多年来一直怀揣着一份怨恨，而我认为作为记者，我有责任将其公之于众。那是一个圣诞节清晨，她穿着睡衣，被家人和礼物包围着，正做着圣诞节早晨该做的事——什么都不做。就在这时，她的手机震动了一下。她自然以为是亲戚发来的节日祝福。

结果是她的CEO通过Teams发来了一条消息，询问她一个问题。

哦，这不是什么紧急情况，比如"大楼着火了，只有你知道灭火器放在哪里"。这只是一个普通的问题——那种可以等到新年甚至等到宇宙热死亡之前才回答的问题。而她的第一反应不是"多么灵活现代的领导者啊"，而是"我在圣诞节惹祸了吗？"

她至今仍难以原谅这件事。当她告诉我这个故事时，我表示了同情，发出了适当的愤怒声响，然后陷入了小小的内心危机。因为，读者，我就是这个故事中的反派。不是这个特定的故事——我从未在圣诞节当天通过Teams轰炸过任何人——但我是这样一个会在22点47分发送工作邮件的人，带着一种从未考虑过收件人神经系统的平静。

我的辩护理由是——我之前从未需要说出口——电子邮件是一种异步通信方式。这正是它的全部特性。这也是我们喜欢它的原因。因此，我假设如果你不准备查看收件箱，你就不会查看。如果真的有什么紧急情况，我绝不会发邮件——我会发短信、打电话或派送信鸽。

我要给这个辩护理由取一个名字，因为我已经使用了它20年，我认识的所有人也都在使用它：异步免罪声明。这一信念认为，因为一条信息可以等待，它也确实在等待——而收件人在晚上发生的任何事情都与你无关。这听起来严密无漏。这是我所相信的最合理的事情之一。然而，我逐渐接受，这大多是胡扯。

这个礼仪问题比我最初想象的更加复杂。让我们深入探讨一下。

我提出"工作时间"已经不是一个共同现实。如果你是一个照顾者，在孩子睡着后才能真正思考；或者像我一样在丹佛，给都柏林团队发邮件；或者你的大脑简直直到21点才启动，那么"下班时间"就只是时间而已。此外，我通常按照东部时间工作（因为媒体行业的一切都在纽约或洛杉矶），这意味着我在6点发送的邮件在我的纽约编辑那里是合理的8点，而至于这封邮件对我的西海岸编辑意味着什么，就别提了。

微软自己的数据表明这不是一种边缘生活方式。在对2025年微软365活动的分析中，该公司发现到22点，近29%的活跃员工已经回到收件箱，而6点在线的40%的人已经在查看邮件。晚上8点后开始的会议增加了16%。更有趣的是：微软研究发现，远程工作者通常将晚上视为一个安静的补习时间窗口，而混合工作者更可能将这些时间视为压力的来源。同样的时间，完全不同的感受。

（我认为这表明了我们作为社会的健康状况好吗？不，这是一个问题——但解决工作与生活平衡的问题将不得不等到它自己的礼仪专栏，与寻找大爆炸的源头和理解为什么我的奶奶会把她从车库洽购会买来的内衣作为礼物送给我一样成为生命的谜团~）

我想强调的是，作为电子邮件使用者和前IT大学教授，关于电子邮件没有要求即刻回应这一点。它就是这样设计的。如果一条信息需要你立即关注，那它应该是一通电话。收件人有选择权——关闭通知、隐藏徽标、把手机放进抽屉，甚至把手机扔进大海。在我们默默同意的长长的电子邮件礼仪规则中，有一部分是关于读者也需要承担一些责任。

而事实证明，读者可能比情况所需更加紧张。伦敦商学院和康奈尔大学的研究人员发现了一种他们称为"电子邮件紧迫性偏差"的现象。在涉及超过4000名参与者的八项预先注册研究中，他们发现收件人始终高估了发件人对非紧急邮件发送在正常工作时间外的回应速度。因此，我的22点47分的邮件让可怜的同事陷入焦虑的原因，是她自己设定的一个从未存在的截止日期。（此外，我从未担任过任何人的上司。）证明自己清白的时刻！

嗯，某种程度上。

然而，同一项研究发现，这种偏差与真实的压力和较低的幸福感有关。"他们过度反应"这一辩护理由在你是那个让他们有东西过度反应的人时显得非常苍白。不，我没有设定截止日期，但我仍然在别人的脑海中安装了一个截止日期，然后去睡觉了。

还有更早的研究支持这一点。莱海大学、弗吉尼亚理工大学和科罗拉多州立大学的基础研究发现，让人疲惫的不是下班后处理电子邮件的时间，而是对它的期待，这会产生研究人员称为预期压力的东西。即使没有邮件真正到达，他们发现这种随时可用的规范也会阻止人们在脑海中下班。因此，造成的伤害不是我的一封周六邮件。而是我的一封周六邮件让所有人知道周六邮件在这里是可以发生的。

现在到了让我的整个理论崩溃的部分，我要记录下我自己发现了这一点，感谢。

当我的一位编辑在21点给我发邮件时，我每次都会看。不是因为我打算工作——我只是想知道是否紧急。这意味着我多年来一直运用的"他们可以简单地不查看邮件"的前提描述了除了我以外的任何人。这里的关键在于：你可以拒绝回应。但你不能拒绝知道。而知道的部分正是毁掉你正在看的电影的部分。

一些国家已经决定这并不是个人怪癖。澳大利亚的"断开连接"法于2024年8月生效，并于2025年8月扩展至小企业，赋予员工拒绝在工作时间外监控、阅读或回复联系的权利，除非拒绝是不合理的。值得注意的是，该法并未使下班时间联系非法。它只是使忽视你合法——这要么让人安心，要么让人谦卑，取决于你多么享受被回应。

无论是晚上还是周末的邮件是否失礼，几乎从不取决于时间。这场争论几乎都归结为三点：你对那个人的关系，你在要求什么，以及你所在的行业。

同事之间，一封夜间邮件无关紧要。从老板到直接下属，这不是邮件——而是带有主题行的准则。这就是为什么我一直以宽松的标准评分：因为我不是任何人的老板。我的异步理论对我的情况非常适用，但如果落入签发工资单的人之手，就会变得非常危险。如果你对任何人的时间表、薪水或绩效评估有权威，你就不能说"我只是在工作时间工作"。你设定了办公室标准，无论你是否愿意。

我可以告诉你，基于个人经验，给自由职业者或承包商发邮件本身就是一个陷阱：你购买的是可交付成果，而不是星期五的晚上。当你给另一家公司的员工发邮件时，你不知道他们的文化要求是什么。采取保守态度。你是在一个你从未阅读过规则的工作场所里客人。

提问没问题。分配任务有些强硬。批评是犯罪。在重大节日发邮件是绝对不行的。没有人在记录历史中看到"我们明天可以聊聊吗？"这条22点的邮件后能安然入睡。如果真的非常紧急，不要发邮件——发短信或打电话。邮件是一种糟糕的应急工具，这正是让那个圣诞节Teams消息如此荒谬的原因。如果它不值得一通电话，那么它不值得打扰。

对于媒体、医疗、政治或任何带有"突发"标签的行业来说，夜晚不是下班时间——夜晚就是工作。对于一些行业，这可能取决于季节（税务日前的4月份的会计工作与7月的会计工作并不相同），但要知道"我们都在拼命工作"描述的是一个季节，而不是永久许可证。了解你的行业文化和你特定公司的文化。

不，黎明的绕行方法并不能挽救你。6点的邮件就是6点的邮件。在清晨而不是午夜发送并不能让你显得体贴；它只能让你成为一个认为别人的早晨是更软的目标的人。

"计划发送"功能存在。解决方案就在那里。它已经在那里等待我们注意它多年了，像一只金毛猎犬。

如果你不愿意——嗨，我就在这里——那么只需要添加："无需周一前回复"。紧迫性偏差研究人员发现，发件人关于回应期望的一句简短说明能显著减少焦虑。只是不要写"No rush!"然后在周日早上8点跟进，因为现在你不仅无礼，而且还在说谎。

此外，当你真正休息时，设置一个真正的离开办公室的消息，并让它有趣一些，因为这是你一周来留下的最后印象。

在晚上或周末发送工作邮件并不无礼。发送得不好才是无礼。

无礼的表现在于发送邮件时暗示有截止日期，发送给无法忽略你的人，或者在23点发送批评后安然入睡。无礼的表现在于拥有计划发送按钮却拒绝使用它，因为在内心深处，你想因为时间戳获得一点赞赏。与此同时，你的同事正盯着天花板，试图不让自己陷入焦虑。

然而，作为邮件收件人，你也有责任管理自己的时间。在特定时间段内不查看邮件并设定边界是完全可以的。

因此，责任是共同的，但并不均分。收件人在周一前不欠你任何。发件人欠他们一句清楚的话。而拥有更多权力的人欠得更多，这正是CEO在圣诞节清晨发"快速问题"是战争罪行，而我22点47分的故事提案只是一个星期二的原因。

我仍然会发送邮件。异步免罪声明并非完全错误——只是不完整，而一句话可以补全它。"无需周一前回复"是将免罪声明变成真正礼貌的东西，而且只需四个字。我看到了我的收件箱在21点对我的影响，而原来那个盯着天花板的人一直都是我。

《读者文摘》已经发表了数百篇礼仪文章，帮助读者应对不断变化的世界中的沟通问题。我们定期涵盖的主题包括为任何场合发送的最佳信息、看似礼貌的习惯实际上并不礼貌、电子邮件和短信礼仪、商务礼仪、小费礼仪、旅行礼仪等等。我们致力于通过具有专业知识和经验的作者与相关合格专家的协同工作，生产高质量的内容。我们依赖于可靠的初级来源，包括政府和专业组织、学术机构以及我们的作者在适当情况下的个人经历。我们核实所有事实和数据，并通过可信的来源进行支持，并不时复核以确保其准确性和最新性。了解更多关于我们团队、贡献者和编辑政策的信息。

《在晚上或周末发送工作邮件真的无礼吗？》原文发布于《读者文摘》。
articles.summary:
One of my editors has a grudge she’s been nursing for years, and I’ve decided it is my journalistic duty to air it. It was Christmas morning. She was in her pajamas, surrounded by her family and wrapping paper, doing exactly what a person should be doing on Christmas morning, which is nothing. Then her phone buzzed. Naturally, she assumed it was a relative with holiday wishes.

It was her CEO. On Teams. With a question.

Oh, it wasn’t an emergency, like “the building is on fire and you alone know where we keep the extinguisher.” It was just a regular question—the kind that could have waited until January, or frankly, until the heat death of the universe. And her first thought was not: What a flexible, modern leader! Her first thought was: Am I in trouble? On Christmas?!

She is still not over it. And when she told me this story, I nodded sympathetically, made an appropriately outraged noise and then had a small internal crisis. Because reader, I am the villain of this story. Not that specific story—I’ve never Teams-bombed anyone’s Christmas—but I am a person who sends work emails at 10:47 p.m. with the serenity of someone who has never once considered the recipient’s nervous system.

My defense, which I have never had to say out loud until now, is this: Email is asynchronous communication. That’s its whole personality. That’s why we like it. So I assume that if you’re not ready to look at your inbox, you simply won’t look at it. And if something were actually on fire, I’d never email—I’d text or call or send a carrier pigeon.

I’m going to give this defense a name, because I’ve been using it for 20 years and so has everyone I know: the async alibi. It’s the belief that because a message can wait, it does wait—and that whatever happens in the recipient’s evening is therefore none of your business. It sounds airtight. It’s the most reasonable thing I’ve ever believed. It’s also, I’ve come to accept, mostly nonsense.

This etiquette question is trickier than I first thought. Let’s get into it.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

The case for sending a message whenever you want

I will propose that “work hours” stopped being a shared reality some time ago. If you’re a caregiver who does real thinking after bedtime, or you’re in Denver, like me, emailing a team in Dublin, or your brain simply boots up at 9 p.m., then “after hours” is just … hours. Plus, I often work on East Coast time (because everything in media is in New York or L.A.), which means that my very early 6 a.m. email hits my New York City editor’s inbox at a reasonable 8 a.m. her time. Let’s not talk about what my 6 a.m. email does to my West Coast editor.

Microsoft’s own data suggests this isn’t a fringe lifestyle. In its 2025 analysis of Microsoft 365 activity, the company found that by 10 p.m., nearly 29% of active workers are back in their inboxes, and 40% of the people online at 6 a.m. are already reviewing email. Meetings starting after 8 p.m. rose 16% year over year. More interesting: Microsoft Research found that remote workers often experience evening hours as a productive window for quiet catch-up, while hybrid workers are more likely to find those same hours stressful. Same clock. Completely different feelings about it.

(Do I think this says good things about our health as a society? No, it’s a problem—but solving work-life balance will have to wait for its own etiquette column, along with sourcing the Big Bang and understanding why my grandma sent me underwear from garage sales as a gift. ~Life’s mysteries~)

I would like to emphasize, as both an email user and a former college professor of IT, that nothing about an email demands immediacy. It was designed that way. If a message required your attention right now, it would be a phone call. The recipient has options—notifications off, badge hidden, phone in a drawer, phone in the ocean. Somewhere in the long list of email etiquette rules we’ve all silently agreed to, there’s a part about the reader having some responsibility too.

And it turns out that readers are probably more stressed than the situation calls for. Researchers at London Business School and Cornell identified something they call the “email urgency bias.” Across eight preregistered studies with more than 4,000 participants, they found that receivers consistently overestimate how quickly senders expect a response to non-urgent emails sent outside normal work hours. So the poor co-worker spiraling over my 10:47 p.m. message is spiraling about a deadline I never set. (Also, I’ve never been anyone’s boss.) Vindication!

Well. Sort of.

The case for keeping your thumbs to yourself

However, that same research found the bias was linked to genuine stress and lower well-being. “They’re overreacting” is a weak defense when you’re the one who handed them the thing to overreact to. No, I didn’t set a deadline, but I still installed one in someone’s head and went to bed.

There’s older research backing this up too. A foundational study out of Lehigh, Virginia Tech and Colorado State found that it isn’t the time spent on after-hours email that wears people down—it’s the expectation of it, which creates what the researchers call anticipatory stress. Even when no emails actually arrive, they found that the mere norm of availability keeps people from mentally clocking out. So the damage isn’t done by my one Saturday email. It’s done by my one Saturday email teaching everyone that Saturday emails happen here.

And now here’s the part where my whole theory falls apart, which I would like the record to show I discovered myself, thank you.

When one of my editors emails me at 9 p.m., I look. Every time. Not because I plan to work—I just need to know whether it’s urgent. Which means the entire “they simply won’t check it” premise I’ve been running on for years describes exactly nobody, including me. Here’s the rub: You can decline to respond. You cannot decline to know. And knowing is the part that ruins the movie you were watching.

Some countries have decided this isn’t a personal quirk at all. Australia’s right-to-disconnect law took effect in August 2024 and expanded to small businesses in August 2025, giving employees the right to refuse to monitor, read or reply to contact outside their working hours, unless that refusal is unreasonable. Notably, it doesn’t make after-hours contact illegal. It just makes ignoring you legal—which is either reassuring or humbling, depending on how much you enjoy being answered.

What actually decides it

Whether a night or weekend email is rude almost never depends on the clock. Almost all of this debate comes down to three things: who you are to the person, what you’re asking and what business you’re in.

Your position

Peer to peer, a night email is a nonevent. From a boss to a direct report, it isn’t an email—it’s a norm with a subject line. This is why I’ve been grading myself on a generous curve: because I’m nobody’s boss. My async theory works beautifully for me, and yet it would be actively harmful in the hands of someone who signs paychecks. If you have authority over anyone’s schedule, salary or performance review, you don’t get to say “I’m just working when I work.” You’re setting the office standards, whether you mean to or not.

And I can tell you from personal experience that emailing a freelancer or contractor is its own trap: You’ve purchased a deliverable, not a Friday night. When you’re emailing someone at another company entirely, you have no idea what their culture demands. Be conservative. You’re a guest in a workplace whose rules you’ve never read.

The topic

A question is fine. A task is pushy. Criticism is a crime. Anything on a major holiday is a hard no. Nobody in recorded history has read “Can we talk tomorrow?” at 10 p.m. and then slept peacefully. And if it’s genuinely urgent, don’t email at all—text or call. Email is a terrible tool for emergencies, which is what made that Christmas Teams ping so absurd. If it wasn’t worth a phone call, then it wasn’t worth the interruption.

Your field

For fields like media, hospitality, health care, live events, politics or anything with a “breaking” tag, night isn’t after hours—night is the job. For some fields, this may depend on the season (accounting in April, right before tax day, is not the same as accounting in July), but know that “we’re all hustling” describes a season, not a permanent license. Know the culture of your field and your particular company.

And no, the sunrise workaround doesn’t save you. A 6 a.m. email is a 6 a.m. email. Sending at dawn instead of midnight doesn’t make you considerate; it makes you someone who decided other people’s mornings were a softer target.

The fixes are embarrassingly easy

“Schedule send” exists. The solution is right there. It’s been right there for years, waiting patiently for us to notice it, like a golden retriever.

And if you can’t be bothered—hi, it’s me—then just add: “No response needed until Monday.” The urgency-bias researchers found that one small clarifying note from the sender about response expectations meaningfully reduced the anxiety. Just don’t write “No rush!” and then follow up at 8 a.m. on Sunday, because now you’re not merely rude, you’re a liar.

Also, set an actual out-of-office message when you’re actually off, and make it a funny one, since it’s the last impression you’ll leave for a week.

So … is it really rude?

Sending a work email at night or on the weekend is not rude. Sending it badly is.

Rude is sending it with an implied deadline, sending it to someone who can’t afford to ignore you, or sending criticism at 11 p.m. and then sleeping soundly. Rude is having a schedule-send button and refusing to press it because, deep down, you’d like a little credit for the time stamp. Meanwhile, your co-worker is staring at the ceiling trying not to spiral.

However, as an email receiver, you should take responsibility for your time. It is OK to draw boundaries with work and let everyone know you won’t be checking email between certain hours.

So the onus is shared—but it isn’t split evenly. The recipient owes you nothing until Monday. The sender owes them one sentence of clarity. And whoever has more power owes more, which is the entire reason a CEO’s Christmas morning “quick question” is a war crime and my 10:47 p.m. story pitch is just a Tuesday.

I’m still going to send them. The async alibi isn’t wrong, exactly—it’s just incomplete, and one sentence completes it. “No response needed until Monday” is the thing that turns an alibi into an actual courtesy, and it costs four words. I’ve seen what my inbox does to me at 9 p.m., and it turns out the ceiling-starer was me all along.

Why trust us

Reader’s Digest has published hundreds of etiquette stories that help readers navigate communication in a changing world. We regularly cover topics such as the best messages to send for any occasion, polite habits that aren’t as polite as they seem, email and texting etiquette, business etiquette, tipping etiquette, travel etiquette and more. We’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. Read more about our team, our contributors and our editorial policies.
